units.title: Topics common to Paper 1 and Paper 2

outcomes.text: Recall the formulae of elements, simple compounds and ions.
Write word equations for reactions.
Write balanced chemical equations with state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq).
Write balanced ionic equations.
Describe how hazard symbols show the dangers of a substance and the safe-working precautions needed.
Evaluate the risks in a practical and suggest suitable precautions.
Describe how Dalton's atom model changed as subatomic particles were discovered.
Describe an atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells.
Recall the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, neutron and electron.
Explain why atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons.
Describe the nucleus as very small compared with the whole atom.
Recall that most of an atom's mass is in the nucleus.

subtopics.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes

outcomes.text: Recall what the mass number of an atom means.
Describe atoms of one element as having the same number of protons, unique to that element.
Describe isotopes as atoms of one element with the same protons but different neutrons.
Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from atomic and mass numbers.
Explain why isotopes make some relative atomic masses not whole numbers.
Calculate an element's relative atomic mass from isotope masses and abundances.
Describe how Mendeleev arranged the known elements using their properties and compounds' properties.
Describe how Mendeleev used his table to predict undiscovered elements and their properties.
Explain why Mendeleev's mass order sometimes failed, because of isotope abundances.
Explain atomic number as an element's position in the table and its number of protons.
Describe the table as ordered by atomic number in periods, with similar elements in groups.
Identify metals and non-metals by position and explain the division using atomic structure.
Predict the electronic configurations of the first 20 elements as diagrams and in the form 2.8.1.
Explain how an element's electronic configuration relates to its position in the table.
Explain how ionic bonds form by electron transfer, using dot and cross diagrams.
Recall that an ion is an atom or group of atoms with a charge.
Calculate the protons, neutrons and electrons in simple ions.
Explain ion formation in compounds of groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 elements.

subtopics.title: Names, formulae and structure of ionic compounds

outcomes.text: Explain the use of the endings -ide and -ate in compound names.
Deduce formulae of ionic compounds from the formulae of their ions.
Explain an ionic compound as a lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic forces.
Explain how a covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons.
Recall that covalent bonding makes molecules.
Recall the typical size, as an order of magnitude, of atoms and small molecules.

subtopics.title: Dot and cross diagrams of molecules

outcomes.text: Draw dot and cross diagrams for hydrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, methane, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Classify substances as ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent or metallic and link structure to properties.
Explain ionic compounds' high melting points and when they conduct electricity.
Explain simple molecular compounds' low melting points and poor conductivity.
Recall that graphite and diamond are forms of carbon and giant covalent substances.
Describe the structures of graphite and diamond.
Explain why graphite makes electrodes and lubricants but diamond makes cutting tools.
Explain the properties of fullerenes such as C60, and graphene, from their structures.
Describe simple polymers, using poly(ethene), as long chains of carbon atoms.
Explain metals' properties, including malleability and electrical conductivity.
Describe the limitations of dot and cross, ball and stick, and 2D/3D models.
Describe typical properties of metals compared with non-metals.
Calculate relative formula mass and percentage by mass of an element in a compound.
Calculate simple compounds' formulae from reacting masses or percentage composition (empirical formulae).
Deduce empirical formula from molecular formula, and molecular formula from empirical formula and relative molecular mass.
Describe an experiment to find the empirical formula of a compound such as magnesium oxide.

subtopics.title: Conservation of mass and reacting masses

outcomes.text: Explain conservation of mass in closed systems and in open flasks where gas is gained or lost.
Calculate masses of reactants and products from a balanced equation.
Calculate the concentration of a solution in g per dm3.
Recall that a mole is the Avogadro number of particles, or the relative particle mass in grams.
Calculate moles from mass, particles from moles, and particles from mass, and the reverse.
Explain why the product mass is set by the reactant that is not in excess.
Deduce a reaction's stoichiometry from the masses of reactants and products.

units.title: Topic 2 - States of matter and mixtures

outcomes.text: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Recall names for state changes and that they are physical changes, unlike chemical reactions.
Explain how particle arrangement, movement and energy change during state changes.
Predict a substance's physical state under given conditions from data.

topics.title: Methods of separating and purifying substances

outcomes.text: Explain how "pure" differs in chemistry and everyday use, and how a pure substance differs from a mixture.
Interpret melting point data to tell pure substances (sharp melting) from mixtures (melting over a range).
Explain which mixtures simple distillation, fractional distillation, filtration, crystallisation and paper chromatography separate.
Choose a suitable technique to separate a mixture from its components' properties.
Describe paper chromatography with a mobile solvent and stationary paper phase.
Interpret a chromatogram to judge purity, identify substances by comparison, and use Rf values.
Investigate the composition of inks using simple distillation and paper chromatography (core practical).
Describe making waste, ground and sea water potable, and why analysis water must be salt-free.
Recall that acids in solution give hydrogen ions and alkalis give hydroxide ions.
Recall that pH 7 is neutral, acids have lower pH and alkalis higher.
Recall the effect of acids and alkalis on litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein.
Recall that more hydrogen ions means lower pH, and more hydroxide ions means higher pH.
Recall that a tenfold rise in hydrogen ion concentration lowers pH by 1.
Investigate the pH change when calcium hydroxide or oxide is added to dilute hydrochloric acid (core practical).
Explain the terms dilute and concentrated.
Explain weak and strong acids in terms of degree of dissociation.
Recall that a base reacts with an acid to form only a salt and water.
Recall that alkalis are soluble bases.
Explain acid reactions with metals, metal oxides, hydroxides and carbonates to make salts.
Describe the tests for hydrogen and for carbon dioxide using limewater.
Describe neutralisation as a reaction between an acid and a base.
Explain neutralisation as hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to form water.
Explain why excess insoluble reactant is added and removed when making a salt from an acid.
Explain why titration and correct proportions are needed for a salt from an acid and a soluble reactant.
Investigate preparing pure dry hydrated copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide using a water bath (core practical).
Describe an acid-alkali titration with burette, pipette and indicator to make a pure dry salt.
Recall the solubility rules for sodium, potassium, ammonium salts, nitrates, chlorides, sulfates, carbonates and hydroxides.
Predict from solubility rules whether a precipitate forms and name it.
Describe how to prepare a pure dry sample of an insoluble salt.
Recall that electrolytes are ionic compounds molten or dissolved in water.
Describe electrolysis as direct current decomposing an electrolyte.
Explain cations moving to the cathode and anions to the anode.
Explain the products of electrolysing copper chloride, sodium chloride, sodium sulfate, acidified water and molten lead bromide.
Predict the products of electrolysing other molten binary ionic compounds.
Write half equations for the reactions at the anode and cathode.
Explain oxidation and reduction as loss and gain of electrons.
Recall that reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode.
Explain the products of electrolysing copper sulfate with copper electrodes and how this purifies copper.
Investigate electrolysis of copper sulfate with inert and copper electrodes (core practical).
Deduce the relative reactivity of metals from their reactions with water, acids and salt solutions.
Explain displacement reactions as redox in terms of electron gain or loss.
Explain the reactivity series using reactions with water and acid and the tendency to form cations.
Recall that most metals come from ores, while unreactive metals occur uncombined.
Explain oxidation as gain of oxygen and reduction as loss of oxygen.
Recall that extracting metals involves reducing ores.
Explain how the extraction method depends on reactivity and cost, using carbon heating and electrolysis.
Evaluate biological extraction methods: bacterial and phytoextraction.
Explain how a metal's resistance to oxidation relates to its place in the reactivity series.
Evaluate the economic and environmental advantages of recycling metals.
Describe a life-cycle assessment covering raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal.
Evaluate data from a life-cycle assessment of a product.
Recall that reactions can be reversible, shown by the symbol, and conditions can change their direction.
Explain what dynamic equilibrium means.
Describe ammonia formation from nitrogen and hydrogen as a reversible reaction reaching dynamic equilibrium.
Recall the Haber process conditions: 450 C, 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst.
Predict how temperature, pressure and concentration changes shift the position of equilibrium.
Recall typical transition metal properties: high melting point, high density, coloured compounds, catalytic activity.
Recall that oxidation of metals causes corrosion.
Explain how rusting is prevented by excluding oxygen or water, or by sacrificial protection.
Explain how electroplating improves appearance or corrosion resistance.
Explain with models why alloys are often stronger than pure metals.
Explain why iron is alloyed to make alloy steels.
Explain how uses of aluminium, copper, gold and alloys such as magnalium and brass relate to their properties.
Calculate concentration in mol per dm3 and convert between g per dm3 and mol per dm3.
Carry out an accurate acid-alkali titration with burette, pipette and indicator (core practical).
Use titration results to calculate an unknown concentration or volume.
Calculate percentage yield from actual and theoretical yield.
Describe why actual yield is usually lower: incomplete reaction, practical losses, side reactions.
Recall what atom economy of a reaction means.
Calculate the atom economy of a reaction.
Explain choosing a reaction pathway using atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium and by-product usefulness.
Describe molar volume as the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure.
Use molar volume and balanced equations for calculations with masses of solids and volumes of gases.
Use Avogadro's law to calculate gas volumes in a gaseous reaction.

subtopics.title: The Haber process and industrial conditions

outcomes.text: Describe the Haber process as a reversible reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen forming ammonia.
Predict how temperature, pressure, concentration and a catalyst affect how fast equilibrium is reached.
Explain how industrial conditions relate to raw material and energy cost and to yield in acceptable time.
Recall that fertilisers contain nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds to promote plant growth.
Describe how ammonia reacts with nitric acid to make a fertiliser salt.
Compare laboratory and industrial production of ammonium sulfate.
Recall that a chemical cell gives a voltage until a reactant is used up.
Recall that a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell gives a voltage with water as the only product.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of fuel cells for given uses.

units.title: Topic 6 - Groups in the periodic table

outcomes.text: Explain why elements are classed as alkali metals, halogens or noble gases from their position.
Recall that alkali metals are soft with relatively low melting points.
Describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water.
Describe the reactivity pattern of alkali metals with water and predict other alkali metals.
Explain the alkali metal reactivity pattern using electronic configurations.
Recall the colours and physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Describe the pattern in halogen physical properties and predict other halogens.
Describe the chemical test for chlorine.
Describe halogen reactions with metals to form metal halides and predict other halogens.
Recall that halogens form hydrogen halides that dissolve to give acidic solutions.
Describe halogen displacement reactions with halide ions and predict astatine's behaviour.
Explain halogen displacement as redox, identifying what is oxidised and reduced.
Explain the relative reactivity of halogens using electronic configurations.
Explain why noble gases are inert in terms of electronic configuration.
Explain how noble gas uses depend on inertness, low density or non-flammability.
Describe the pattern in noble gas physical properties and predict others.

units.title: Topic 7 - Rates of reaction and energy changes

outcomes.text: Investigate how conditions affect rates by measuring gas produced and observing a colour change (core practical).
Suggest practical methods for measuring the rate of a reaction.
Explain reactions occurring by particle collisions and rates rising with collision frequency or energy.
Explain the effects of temperature, concentration, surface area and pressure on rate using collisions.
Interpret graphs of mass, volume or concentration against time.
Describe a catalyst as speeding up a reaction while unchanged itself.
Explain how a catalyst raises rate by lowering activation energy.
Recall that enzymes are biological catalysts used in making alcoholic drinks.

topics.title: Heat energy changes in chemical reactions

outcomes.text: Recall heat changes in dissolving, neutralisation, displacement and precipitation, measured as temperature changes.
Describe an exothermic reaction as giving out heat energy.
Describe an endothermic reaction as taking in heat energy.
Recall that breaking bonds is endothermic and making bonds is exothermic.
Recall that overall heat change depends on energy released making bonds versus energy needed breaking bonds.
Calculate a reaction's energy change from bond energies.
Explain the term activation energy.
Draw and label reaction profiles for endothermic and exothermic reactions, showing activation energy.
Recall that hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
Describe crude oil as a mixture of hydrocarbons, a source of fuels and feedstock, and finite.
Describe and explain separating crude oil by fractional distillation.
Recall the names and uses of the gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen fractions.
Explain how fractions differ in molecule size, boiling point, ease of ignition and viscosity.
Explain a homologous series: general formula, CH2 difference, gradual property change, similar chemistry.
Describe complete combustion of hydrocarbons giving carbon dioxide, water and energy.
Explain how incomplete combustion produces carbon and carbon monoxide.
Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
Describe problems of carbon monoxide and soot from incomplete combustion in appliances.
Explain how fuel impurities produce sulfur dioxide.
Explain problems of acid rain from sulfur dioxide.
Explain how engines make oxides of nitrogen from oxygen and nitrogen at high temperature.
Evaluate using hydrogen rather than petrol as a car fuel.
Recall that petrol, kerosene, diesel and methane are non-renewable fossil fuels.
Explain cracking as breaking large alkanes into smaller, useful molecules including alkenes.
Explain why cracking is necessary.
Recall that volcanic gases formed the early atmosphere.
Describe the early atmosphere as little oxygen, much carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases, and interpret evidence.
Explain how condensing water vapour formed the oceans.
Explain how carbon dioxide fell as it dissolved in the forming oceans.
Explain how primitive plants used carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis.
Describe the chemical test for oxygen.
Describe how carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb heat radiated from Earth: the greenhouse effect.
Evaluate the evidence that human activity causes climate change, including its uncertainties.
Describe today's atmosphere, climate effects of extra carbon dioxide and methane, and how these might be mitigated.
Explain why the test for any ion must be unique.
Describe flame tests for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions.
Describe sodium hydroxide tests for aluminium, calcium, copper, iron(II), iron(III) and ammonium ions.
Describe the chemical test for ammonia.
Describe tests for carbonate, sulfate, chloride, bromide and iodide ions.
Identify the ions in unknown salts using the ion tests (core practical).
Identify the ions in unknown salts from test results.
Describe how instrumental analysis can improve sensitivity, accuracy and speed.
Evaluate flame photometer data to find ion concentration from a calibration curve or identify metal ions.
Recall the formulae of methane, ethane, propane and butane and draw their structures.
Explain why alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons.
Recall the formulae of ethene, propene and butene and draw their structures.
Explain why alkenes are unsaturated, with the C=C functional group.
Recall the addition reaction of ethene with bromine and extend it to other alkenes.
Explain how bromine water distinguishes alkanes from alkenes.
Describe complete combustion of alkanes and alkenes as oxidation giving carbon dioxide and water.
Recall that a polymer is a high-mass substance made of small repeating units.
Describe how ethene molecules join to make poly(ethene) in addition polymerisation.
Describe making poly(propene), PVC and PTFE from monomers containing C=C.
Deduce a monomer from an addition polymer structure and vice versa.
Explain how uses of poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC and PTFE relate to their properties.
Explain why polyesters are condensation polymers, formed from diacid and dialcohol monomers with water released.
Describe problems with polymers: starting materials, landfill persistence, combustion gases, sorting.
Evaluate the pros and cons of recycling polymers.
Recall that DNA, starch and proteins are natural polymers of nucleotides, sugars and amino acids.
Recall the formulae of methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol and draw their structures.
Recall that the alcohol functional group is -OH and alcohols can be dehydrated to alkenes.
Investigate the temperature rise from burning ethanol, propanol, butanol and pentanol (core practical).
Recall the formulae of methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acids and draw their structures.
Recall that the functional group is -COOH and carboxylic acid solutions are acidic.
Recall that ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid, and extend this to other alcohols.
Recall that members of a homologous series react similarly because of the same functional group, and predict products.
Describe making ethanol by fermenting carbohydrates with yeast.
Explain how fractional distillation concentrates ethanol from a fermentation mixture.

topics.title: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles

outcomes.text: Compare the size of nanoparticles with atoms and molecules.
Describe how nanoparticle properties, including surface area to volume ratio, relate to uses such as sunscreens.
Explain the possible risks of some nanoparticulate materials.
Compare physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals using data.
Explain why a material's properties suit a use, and use data to select materials.
